title: The Security Flag in the IPv4 Header
summary: An April 1st joke RFC. It proposes a bit in the IPv4 header that senders set to 1 if the packet has malicious intent, so firewalls could tell bad packets from merely unusual ones. The humor is that attackers would never honestly set it. It is an informational April Fools memo and not a real protocol.

eli5.summary: Imagine every sneaky person had to wear a sign saying I am sneaky. That is the joke here: a flag on bad network traffic that bad guys are asked to turn on. It was published as an April Fools prank.

questions: where is the evil bit in the ipv4 header
what does the evil bit do
subtitle: An April 1st joke: a single header bit that attackers are supposed to set to 1 to announce evil intent.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and intrusion detection systems struggle to tell malicious packets from merely unusual ones.
tldr.mechanism: Define the high-order bit of the IPv4 fragment offset field as the "evil" bit: 0 for harmless packets, 1 for packets used in an attack. Firewalls drop inbound packets with the bit set.
tldr.outcome: It is an April 1st joke. The punchline is that attackers would have to label their own packets, and the memo says as much in its security considerations.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: High-order bit of the IP fragment offset field

today: RFC 3514 is an Informational April 1st joke document, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is not a real protocol.

sections.title: An April 1st Proposal
sections.content: RFC 3514 is an April 1st joke document, dated 1 April 2003. It is written with a perfectly straight face. It notes that firewalls, packet filters and intrusion detection systems have trouble telling packets with malicious intent from merely unusual ones, and solves it by defining a security flag, the evil bit, in the IPv4 header. Benign packets have it set to 0; attack packets set it to 1.
sections.eli5: The grown-ups say: let bad guys put a sticker on their mail that says bad. It is a joke because bad guys would not.

sections.title: The Evil Bit
sections.content:
The high-order bit of the IP fragment offset field is the only unused bit in the IP header, so the memo says the bit position is not left to IANA. The field is one bit wide, labelled E.

With 0x0, the packet has no evil intent and hosts SHOULD assume it is harmless and SHOULD NOT take defensive measures. The RFC jokes that many common desktop operating systems already implement this part. With 0x1, the packet has evil intent: secure systems SHOULD try to defend themselves, and insecure systems MAY choose to crash, be penetrated, and so on.
sections.eli5: One tiny switch: off means friendly, on means up to no good.

sections.title: Setting and Processing the Bit
sections.content:
Attack applications MUST set the bit, and systems without other mechanisms MUST provide an API for it. Fragments that are dangerous by themselves MUST carry the bit. Hosts inside a firewall MUST NOT set it, because the memo calls it axiomatic that all attackers are outside. NAT boxes and transparent proxies SHOULD set it on packets they modify or reply with.

Firewalls MUST drop all inbound packets with the bit set and MUST NOT drop packets with it off. Intrusion detection systems MUST apply a probabilistic correction factor, consulting a random number generator to decide whether to log. Routers not intended as security devices SHOULD NOT examine the bit, so they can pass packets at higher speeds.
sections.eli5: Guards at the gate turn away anyone wearing the bad badge, and let everyone else in. Mail sorters who are not guards do not bother looking.

sections.title: Related Work and Security
sections.content:
The memo sketches complementary mechanisms for other forms of evil: two IPv6 options (hop-by-hop and end-to-end) carrying a 128-bit strength indicator and a 128-bit type code, an evil lambda or polarization for optical links, a special diffserv code point for DDoS packets, and an application/evil MIME type.

Its security considerations note that security mechanisms depend critically on the bit being set properly. If faulty components fail to set it, firewalls cannot do their jobs. If it is set when it should not be, a denial of service may result. For behavior of other values, the IANA section allows definition only by IETF consensus.
sections.eli5: If the bad guys forget the badge, the guards cannot help. If someone puts the badge on a good person by mistake, that person gets turned away.
